<meta>This page serves as the preface to the first volume of the Old Testament in the reduced photographic facsimile of the Codex Alexandrinus. It establishes continuity with the 1909 New Testament volume and introduces the specific scribal characteristics of the Octateuch.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION

THE general Introduction to the reduced photographic facsimile of the Codex Alexandrinus <note>A famous 5th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible, one of the four great uncial codices.</note> is prefixed to the part containing the New Testament and the Clementine Epistles, issued in 1909. In that Introduction is given the history of the manuscript, so far as it is known, and of the various editions of it, a statement of its contents, and an analysis of the various hands of the scribes and correctors employed upon it. To this there is little that is material to be added here.<sup>1</sup>

The present part (the first of four that will contain the Old Testament) comprises the Octateuch <note>The first eight books of the Old Testament: Genesis through Ruth.</note>. These eight books form a single unit, written by a single scribe. They are also the part of the manuscript which has been most extensively corrected. As has been stated in the general Introduction, the original readings of the MS. <note>Manuscript</note>, and the work of the various correctors, are indicated as follows:

->A = the reading of the MS. when there has been no alteration.<-
->A* = the original reading of the MS. when there has been an alteration.<-
->A<sup>1</sup> = the reading of the correction, when it has been made by the original scribe.<-
->A<sup>a</sup>, A<sup>b</sup>, A<sup>c</sup>, &c. = readings due to subsequent correctors.<-

The attributions of the various corrections to their several authors, so far as the present editor has been able to satisfy himself on the subject, are recorded in the larger Cambridge edition of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>.<sup>2</sup> Most of them are due either to the original scribe or to the first corrector (A<sup>a</sup>), whose hand (visible on an un-erased portion of the vellum) is smoother and rounder than that of his predecessors, but does not appear to be materially later in date. This corrector worked very drastically on the earlier books of the Octateuch, frequently erasing whole passages of two, three, or four lines, and substituting a fresh text. The textual relation of the corrector to the original scribe does not appear to have been studied as yet, but the material is now available in the edition of Messrs. Brooke and McLean, and (substantially) in the earlier edition of Dr. Swete. It is possible that a study of this subject would assist in determining the authorship of certain of the corrections, where the palaeographical <note>The study of ancient handwriting.</note> indications are doubtful. The work of the other correctors (of whom three may be discerned) is of very minor importance.

F. G. KENYON.

BRITISH MUSEUM,
*15 Jan., 1915.*

---

<sup>1</sup> Prof. Burkitt, in a review of the New Testament volume (*Journal of Theological Studies*, xi. 603, 1910), has some interesting remarks, favouring the tradition recorded by Wetstein (see N. T., Introduction, p. 7, note 3) to the effect that the manuscript was found at Mt. Athos. In his opinion, the Arabic note by “Athanasius the humble” may be contemporary with Cyril, and the work of one of his staff; the MS. may never have been in Egypt at all until Cyril brought it there, but may be of Constantinopolitan origin, which would account for the Constantinopolitan character of its text in the Gospels. If an Arabic scholar and palaeographer states that it is not possible to be certain whether a note was written in the fourteenth or the seventeenth century, it is not for those who have no knowledge of Oriental palaeography to dispute the statement; but it does seem absolutely impossible to believe that Cyril <note>Cyril Lucaris (1572–1638), Patriarch of Alexandria and later of Constantinople, who gave the Codex to King Charles I.</note> had himself brought the MS. from Athos to Alexandria. If Cyril had himself found it at Athos, and presented it to the patriarchate at Alexandria with an anathema on its removal, it is not very likely that he would have transferred it to Constantinople, and still less likely that he would have impressed its Egyptian origin on Sir Thomas Roe (as he evidently did), and suppressed its Athoan derivation and his own merit in discovering it. But even if these difficulties are ignored, it is plainly incredible that he should with his own hand have stated its Egyptian origin, as he does in the autograph note prefixed to the manuscript, and should have attributed the mutilation of the end of the MS. to the ill-treatment which the Christians and their books suffered after the Mahomedan conquest of Egypt. This note makes it certain that Cyril himself believed in the Egyptian origin of the MS.; and in face of this evidence, the statement of his deacon, Matthaeus Muttis, falls to the ground. One is tempted to say that Prof. Burkitt’s suggestion has only the attractiveness of the improbable.

<sup>2</sup> *The Old Testament in Greek . . .*, edited by A. E. Brooke, B.D., and N. McLean, M.A., Vol. I, part i (Cambridge, 1906).

<summary>This introduction by F.G. Kenyon describes the first volume of the Old Testament facsimile of the Codex Alexandrinus, focusing on the scribal corrections within the Octateuch. Kenyon also argues against the theory that the manuscript originated at Mt. Athos, defending its traditional Egyptian provenance.</summary>
<keywords>Codex Alexandrinus, Octateuch, Septuagint, scribal corrections, Cyril Lucaris, F.G. Kenyon, manuscript provenance, Alexandria, Mt. Athos</keywords>

<meta>This page follows the table of contents of the first volume. It contains a significant historical inscription by Cyril Lucaris, the 17th-century Patriarch of Constantinople, regarding the origins of this specific manuscript—the Codex Alexandrinus. The note attempts to authenticate the manuscript by linking it to the early Christian saint, Thecla. While the source language is identified as Greek in the header, the text provided for translation is written in Latin.</meta>

This <unclear>manuscript</unclear>, the <unclear>sacred</unclear> scripture <gloss>of the</gloss> N[ew] and O[ld] Testam[ent] <gloss>as</gloss> <note>original: "N. et V. testam:"; an abbreviation for "Novi et Veteris Testamenti."</note> we have it from tradition, was written by the hand of Thecla, a noble Egyptian woman, about one thousand three hundred years ago, shortly after the Council of Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea, held in 325 AD, was a pivotal gathering of Christian bishops. Lucaris is dating the manuscript to the 4th century based on this tradition.</note>. The name <gloss>of</gloss> Thecla was inscribed at the end of the book; but when Christianity was extinguished in Egypt by the Muslims <note>original: "Mahometanis"; a historical term used by the author to refer to the Islamic conquest and subsequent era.</note>, and the books of the Christians were brought to a similar state of ruin, the name of Thecla was also erased <gloss>and</gloss> torn away. However, memory and tradition still preserve it.

->† Cyril, Patriarch of Constantinople <gloss>p</gloss><-

<summary>This page contains a signed attestation by Patriarch Cyril Lucaris claiming that the manuscript was written by St. Thecla in the 4th century. He explains that her signature was lost during historical upheavals in Egypt, but her authorship remains known through tradition.</summary>

### Genesis 11:8–31

And the Lord <note>original: "KC̅" (Kyrios), a shortened form used by scribes for "Lord".</note> scattered them from there upon the face of all the earth, and they ceased building the city and the tower. Because of this, its name was called **Confusion** <term>sygchysis: the Greek translation of the Hebrew word 'Babel,' referring to the mixing or confounding of languages</term>, because there the Lord <note>original: "KC̅"</note> confounded the speech <note>original: "cheilē," literally "lips," a common idiom for language</note> of all the earth; and from there the Lord <note>original: "KC̅"</note> scattered them upon the face of all the earth.

Shall not the one who judges all the earth do what is right?"

And the Lord said: "If I find in Sodom fifty righteous men, I will forgive the whole place for their sake."

And Abraham answered and said: "Now I have begun to speak to the Lord, though I am but earth and ashes. <note>original: "gē kai spodos," a classic expression of human humility and mortality.</note> What if the fifty righteous are lacking by five? And he said: "I will not destroy it if I find thirty there."
And he said: "Since I have started to speak to the Lord—what if twenty should be found there?"
And he said: "I will not destroy it for the sake of the twenty."
And he said: "May the Lord not be angry if I speak yet once more—what if ten should be found there?"
And he said: "I will not destroy it for the sake of the ten."

And the Lord departed as soon as he ceased speaking to Abraham; and Abraham returned to his own place.

### The Deception for the Blessing

And **Rebekah** spoke to **Jacob**, her younger son, saying, "Look, I heard your father speaking to **Esau** your brother, saying: 'Bring me game and make me food <note>original: 'edesmata'; refers to a specially prepared savory dish</note>, so that I may eat and bless you before the **Lord** <note>original: 'KY', a sacred abbreviation for 'Kyriou'</note> before I die.'</note>

"Now therefore, my son, listen to me, just as I command you. Go to the sheep and take for me from there two tender and good kids, and I will make them into food for your father, just as he likes. Then you shall bring it to your father and he will eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."

But **Jacob** said to **Rebekah** his mother, "**Esau** my brother is a hairy man, but I am a smooth man. What if my father should feel me? <note>original: 'psēlaphēsē'; to touch or grope, indicating Isaac's blindness</note> I shall be in his sight as one who is a deceiver, and I shall bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing."

And his mother said to him, "Upon me be your curse, my child; only obey my voice and go, bring them to me."

So he went and took them and brought them to his mother, and his mother made food just as his father liked. And **Rebekah** took the fine robe of **Esau** her older son, which was with her in the house, and she dressed **Jacob** her younger son in it. She also placed the skins of the kids upon his arms and upon the bare parts of his neck. Then she gave the food and the bread she had made into the hands of **Jacob** her son. 

And he went in to his father and said, "My father." 

And he said, "Behold, I am here. Who are you, my child?" And **Jacob** said to his father:

## Jacob’s Wages and the Spotted Flocks

And it happened, when Rachel had given birth to **Joseph**, that **Jacob** said to **Laban**, "Send me away so that I may go to my own place and my own land. Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, so that I may go; for you yourself know the service which I have served you."

And Laban said to him, "If I have found favor in your sight, I have learned by omen <note>original: 'οἰωνισάμην' (oiōnisamēn), referring to divination or observing omens</note> that **God** <note>original: 'ΘϹ' (Theos), written as a Nomina Sacra contraction</note> has blessed me because of your coming. Name your wages to me, and I will give them."

But Jacob said to him, "You know how I have served you, and what your livestock has become with me. For what you had before I came was little, and it has increased to a multitude; and the **Lord** <note>original: 'ΚϹ' (Kyrios)</note> has blessed you at my every step <note>original: 'ἐπὶ τῷ ποδί μου', literally 'at my foot'</note>. Now therefore, when shall I also provide for my own house?"

And Laban said to him, "What shall I give you?" And Jacob said to him, "You shall not give me anything; if you will do this thing for me, I will again shepherd your sheep and guard them: Let all your sheep pass by today, and separate from there every dark <note>original: 'φαιὸν' (phaion)</note> sheep among the lambs, and every spotted and white one among the goats—that shall be my wage. And my righteousness shall answer for me on the day of tomorrow, when my wage comes before you; everything that is not spotted and white among the goats and dark among the lambs shall be considered stolen if it is with me."

And Laban said to him, "Let it be according to your word." And he separated on 그 day the spotted and mottled male goats, and all the spotted and mottled female goats, and everything that had white in it, and everything dark among the lambs, and he gave them into the hand of his sons. And he put a distance of a three days' journey between them and Jacob. And Jacob shepherded the sheep of Laban that were left behind.

And Jacob took for himself a rod of green storax-wood <note>original: 'στυρακίνην' (styrakinēn)</note> and of hazel

<column-break/>

and of the plane tree, and Jacob peeled them with white peelings, uncovering the green; and the white appeared on the rods which he had peeled, variegated. And he placed the rods which he had peeled in the troughs of the water-drinkers, so that when the sheep came to drink, they might conceive <note>original: 'ἐνκισσήσωσιν' (enkissēsōsin), meaning to be in heat or to conceive</note> in front of the rods as they came to drink.

And the sheep conceived at the rods, and the sheep brought forth spotted and mottled and ash-colored <note>original: 'σποδοειδῆ' (spodoeidē), literally "looking like ash"</note> streaked ones. And Jacob separated the lambs and set the spotted and all the ash-colored ones in front of the sheep; he separated for himself flocks by himself and did not mix them into the sheep of Laban.

And it happened, in the season when the sheep were conceiving in the womb, that Jacob took the rods and placed them before the sheep in the troughs, so that they might conceive according to the rods. But whenever the sheep brought forth, he did not place them there. So it happened that the unmarked ones belonged to Laban, and the marked ones belonged to Jacob. And the man became exceedingly wealthy, and he had many livestock and cattle, and male and female servants, and camels and donkeys.

# Genesis 37

...because of his dreams and because of his words. 
And he had another dream and described it to his father and to his brothers, saying: "Behold, I have dreamed another dream; it was as if the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me." 

And his father rebuked him and said to him: "What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall we indeed come—I and your mother and your brothers—to bow down before you to the earth?" And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind. 

And his brothers went to graze the sheep of their father in Shechem <note>Shechem was an ancient city in central Canaan, often associated with grazing lands but also a place of previous family conflict.</note>. And Israel <note>original: "ΙΣΡΑΗΛ" — This is another name for Jacob, Joseph's father.</note> said to Joseph: "Are not your brothers shepherding in Shechem? Come, let me send you to them." 

And he said to him: "Behold, here I am." 

And Israel said to him: "Go now, see if your brothers are well and the sheep are well, and bring word back to me." And he sent him out of the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem. 

<margin>¶</margin> And a man found him wandering in the field; and the man asked him, saying: "What are you looking for?" And he said: "I am looking for my brothers; tell me, where are they grazing?" 

And the man said to him: "They have moved on from here, for I heard them saying, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" And Joseph went after his brothers and found them in Dothan. 

And they saw him from a distance before he came near to them, and they plotted wickedly to kill him. And each said to his brother: "Behold, that dreamer <note>original: "Ο ΕΝΥΠΝΙΑΣΤΗΣ" — Literally "the master of dreams," used here with derision.</note> is coming! Now therefore, come, let us kill him...

<column-break/>

...and let us throw him into one of the pits, and we will say that a wild beast has devoured him; and then we shall see what will become of his dreams." 

But when Reuben heard it, he delivered him out of their hands and said: "Let us not strike his life <note>original: "ΕΙΣ ΨΥΧΗΝ" — referring to his soul or his very life.</note>." 

<margin>¶</margin> And Reuben said to them: "Do not shed blood; throw him into one of the pits that are in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him"—so that he might rescue him out of their hands and restore him to his father. 

<margin>¶</margin> And it happened, when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of his ornate tunic <note>original: "ΧΙΤΩΝΑ ΤΟΝ ΠΟΙΚΙΛΟΝ" — Often translated as "coat of many colors," it refers to a long-sleeved or richly decorated garment signifying status.</note> that he was wearing. And they took him and threw him into the pit; now the pit was empty, it had no water. 

And they sat down to eat bread. And looking up with their eyes, they saw, and behold, Ishmaelite travelers <note>The Ishmaelites were descendants of Ishmael, Abraham's other son, often appearing as desert traders.</note> were coming from Gilead, and their camels were loaded with incense and resin and stacte <note>term: "stacte" — A precious, fragrant oil or resin, often used as an ingredient in holy incense.</note>; they were on their way to carry them down to Egypt. 

<margin>¶</margin> And Judah said to his brothers: "What is the use if we kill our brother and hide his blood? Come, let us sell him to these Ishmaelites, and let our hands not be upon him, for he is our brother and our own flesh." 

And his brothers listened to him. And Midianite merchants <note>note: The text mentions both Ishmaelites and Midianites; they are often used interchangeably in this passage to describe the group of traders.</note> were passing by, and they pulled Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of gold <note>original: "ΕΙΚΟΣΙ ΧΡΥΣΩΝ" — While most versions say silver, this manuscript specifies gold.</note>. And they took Joseph down into Egypt. 

Now Reuben returned to the pit, and he did not see Joseph in the pit; and he tore his clothes.

# Genesis 38–39

He turned aside toward her on the road and said to me <note>The Greek text here says "to me," which may be a scribe's error for "to her," or reflecting a different manuscript tradition.</note>, for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. But she said, "Only if you give me a pledge <term>arrhabōn: a security deposit or down payment used to guarantee a future transaction</term> until you send it."

And he said, "What pledge shall I give you?" She said, "Your signet ring, and the cord, and the staff in your hand." And he gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him. And rising up, she departed and took off her veil from her and put on the garments of her widowhood.

Judah sent the young goat by the hand of his shepherd, the Adullamite, to recover the pledge from the woman, but he did not find her. He asked the men of that place, saying, "Where is the prostitute <note>original: "Η ΠΟΡΝΗ" — The Greek text uses a word for a common prostitute, though the context often implies a cultic or shrine prostitute.</note> who was at Enaim by the road?" And the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a successful man; and he was in the house of his master, the Egyptian.

His master knew that the Lord was with him, and that the Lord made everything he did prosper in his hands. Joseph found favor in the sight of his master and pleased him; and he appointed him over his house and entrusted all that he had into Joseph's hand. 

It happened after he appointed him over his house and over all his possessions, that the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house because of Joseph; the blessing of the Lord was upon all his possessions in the house and in the field. And he left everything he had in Joseph's hands; he did not concern himself with anything except the bread that he ate. 

Now Joseph was handsome in form and very beautiful in appearance.

# Genesis 41

The seven years of abundance that occurred in the land of Egypt passed away. And the seven years of famine began to arrive, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all the earth, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread. When all the land of Egypt hungered, the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread.

# Genesis 42

<margin>42 ~</margin>

When Jacob saw that there was a sale in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why are you idle? Look, I have heard there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy a little food for us, so that we may live and not die."

So Joseph's ten brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt. But Benjamin, Joseph's brother, he did not send with his brothers, for he said, "Lest some misfortune <note>original: "μαλακια" — literally 'softness' or 'weakness,' here referring to an accident or illness.</note> befall him."

Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, but he acted like a stranger to them and spoke harshly to them. He said to them, "Where have you come from?" They said, "From the land of Canaan to buy food."

<column-break/>

Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him. And Joseph remembered the dreams which he had seen, and he said to them, "You are spies! You have come to inspect the lookout points <note>original: "τα σκοπους" — the vantage points or vulnerable entrances of a country.</note> of the country."

But they said, "No, lord, your servants have come to buy food. We are all sons of one man; we are peaceful men. Your servants are not spies."

But he said to them, "No, rather you have come to see the tracks <note>original: "τα ίχνη" — the footprints or secret paths</note> of the region."

They said, "We, your servants, are twelve brothers in the land of Canaan, and look, the youngest is with our father today, and the other one no longer exists."

Joseph said to them, "This is what I told you when I said, 'You are spies.' By this you shall be made manifest: by the health of Pharaoh! <note>original: "νη την υγιαν Φαραω" — an oath invoking the life/health of the king, common in Egyptian court settings.</note> You shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here. Otherwise, by the health of Pharaoh, you are certainly spies."

And he put them in prison for three days. On the third day, Joseph said to them, "Do this and you shall live, for I fear God <note>original: "ΘΝ" — Nomen Sacrum for Θεόν (God).</note>. If you are peaceful men, let one of your brothers be held in the prison, but you go and carry away the grain you have purchased for your households. Bring your youngest brother to me, and your words will be proven trustworthy; otherwise, you shall die."

And they did so.

Then each said to his brother, "Truly we are in sin regarding our brother..."

You shall not join with a multitude to do evil, nor shall you turn aside with the many so as to pervert justice. You shall not show pity to a poor man in judgment <note>The law demands impartiality; one must not favor a person in court simply because they are poor, just as one must not favor the rich.</note>.
If you happen upon the ox of your enemy or his beast of burden wandering, you shall certainly turn it back and return it to him.
If you see the beast of burden belonging to your enemy fallen under its load, you shall not pass it by, but you shall help him raise it up.
You shall not pervert the judgment of a poor man in his lawsuit. Stay far away from every unjust word. You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous, and you shall not justify the ungodly for the sake of gifts <note>original: "δωρων" (dōrōn) — here referring to bribes or payoffs.</note>. ### The Bronze Altar
<margin>[</margin><margin>27</margin>And you shall make an altar of unrotting wood <term>unrotting wood: usually identified as acacia wood, prized in antiquity for its durability and resistance to insects</term>, five cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, approximately 18 inches, based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term> in length and five cubits in width—the altar shall be square—and its height shall be three cubits. And you shall make horns upon its four corners; the horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall cover them with bronze. And you shall <margin>[</margin>make a rim for the altar, and its cover, and its base, and its flesh-hooks, and its fire-pan; all its vessels you shall make of bronze.

<margin>[</margin>And you shall make for it a grate of network <note>original: "ἐσχάραν ἔργῳ δικτυωτῷ" — a bronze lattice or mesh designed to hold the wood and allow ashes to fall through</note> of bronze, and you shall make for the grate four bronze rings at its four corners. And you shall put them under the grate of the altar <margin>[</margin>below; and the grate shall reach to the middle of the altar.

And you shall make poles for the altar of unrotting wood, and you shall overlay <note>original: "χρυσώσεις" — though the word usually means "to gild with gold," the text specifies "with bronze" (χαλκῷ) here, matching the other courtyard items</note> them with bronze, and you shall bring the poles into the rings, and let the poles be

along the sides of the altar when it is carried. You shall make it hollow, of boards; as it was shown to you on the mountain, so shall you make it.

### The Outer Court
<margin>[</margin><note>Section marker (circle with dot)</note> AND YOU SHALL MAKE the court of the tabernacle; on the side toward the southwest <note>original: "λίβα" — the southwest wind, here indicating the southern side of the enclosure</note>, the hangings of the court shall be of spun fine linen, a length of one hundred cubits for the one side. And their pillars shall be twenty, and their bases twenty, made of bronze; and their rings and their fillets <note>original: "ψαλίδες" — decorative bands or connecting rods between pillars</note> shall be silver.

So for the side toward the north, there shall be hangings of one hundred cubits in length; and their pillars shall be <margin>[</margin>twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze; and their rings and the fillets of the pillars and their bases shall be overlaid with silver.

And the width of the court toward the sea <note>original: "θάλασσαν" — the Mediterranean Sea, used as a standard term for "West"</note>, there shall be hangings of fifty cubits; their pillars ten and their bases ten. And the width of the court toward the south, there shall be hangings of fifty cubits; their pillars fifteen and their bases three, fifteen cubits high. For the corner, their pillars shall be three and their bases three.

<margin>[</margin>And for the gate of the court, there shall be a screen of twenty cubits, the work of an embroiderer, of blue and purple and spun scarlet and spun fine linen; their pillars shall be four and their bases four. All the pillars of the court shall be silvered all around with silver, and their capitals shall be silver and their bases bronze.

And the length of the court <margin>[</margin>shall be one hundred by one hundred, and the width fifty by fifty, and the height five cubits, of spun fine linen; and their bases of bronze. And all the <margin>[</margin>equipment of the tabernacle in all its service, and all the pins of the tabernacle and all the pins of the court shall be of bronze.

### The Consecration Ritual and the Daily Offerings

And it shall be for Aaron and his sons a perpetual statute <term>nomimon aiōnion: a law or custom intended to last forever</term> from the children of Israel; for it is a contribution <note>original: "aphairēma" — a portion "lifted off" or set aside from a larger sacrifice to support the priests</note>. And it shall be a contribution from the children of Israel, from the peace offerings <margin>of the Lord</margin> a contribution from <unclear>...</unclear>
<margin>|</margin> And the holy garment which belongs to Aaron shall be for his sons after him, to be anointed in them and to have their hands consecrated <term>literally: "to fulfill the hands," the technical ritual process for ordaining a priest</term>. For seven days, the priest who takes his place from among his sons, who enters into the tent of testimony to minister in the holy place, shall put them on.
<margin>|</margin> And you shall take the ram of consecration and boil its meat in a holy place. And Aaron and his sons shall eat the meat of the ram and the bread that is in the basket by the doors of the tent of testimony. They shall eat those things by which they were sanctified, to consecrate their hands and to hallow them. But no stranger <note>original: "allogenēs" — someone from a different lineage, in this context, a non-priest</note> shall eat of them, for they are holy. And if any of the meat of the sacrifice of consecration or the bread remains until morning, you shall burn the remainder with fire; it shall not be eaten, for it is a holy thing. And thus you shall do for Aaron and his sons according to all that I have commanded you; for seven days you shall consecrate their hands. And you shall offer a calf as a sin offering on the day of purification. And you shall cleanse the altar when you perform the sanctification upon it, and you shall anoint it so as to hallow it. Seven days you shall cleanse the altar and hallow it; and the altar shall be "most holy" <note>literally: "holy of holies"</note>. Everyone who touches the altar <margin>|</margin> shall be sanctified. And these are the things you shall offer upon the altar: two yearling lambs without blemish every day upon the altar as a continual offering.

<column-break/>

As a continual offering, the one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the second lamb you shall offer in the evening. And a tenth of a measure of fine flour mixed with beaten oil, a fourth of a hin <note>original: "in" — a liquid measure of approximately 1.5 gallons</note>, and a drink offering of a fourth of a hin of wine for the one lamb. And the second lamb you shall offer in the evening; according to the morning sacrifice and according to its drink offering you shall do, for a sweet-smelling savor, an offering to the Lord, a continual sacrifice <margin>Chapter 30</margin> <note>The marginal Greek letter lambda (λ) acts as a numeral for 30, marking the beginning of the next chapter</note> throughout your generations at the doors of the tent of testimony before the <margin>|</margin> Lord, where I will be known to you from there, so as to speak to you. And I will there give orders to the children of Israel, and I shall be sanctified in my glory. And I will hallow the tent of testimony and the altar, and I will hallow Aaron and his sons to serve me as priests. And I shall be called upon among the children of Israel and will be their God. And they shall know that I am the Lord their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt to be called upon by them and to be their God. And you shall make an altar of incense <note>original: "thumiamatōn"</note> of rot-proof wood <term>shittim: traditionally acacia wood, valued for its durability</term>. And you shall make it a cubit <note>approximately 18 inches</note> in length and a cubit in width; it shall be square. And its height shall be two cubits; its horns shall be of one piece with it. And you shall overlay it with pure gold—its grate and its walls round about and its horns. And you shall make for it a molded gold border round about.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the Tabernacle's construction, specifically moving from the High Priest's breastplate (described on the previous page) to the inner veil, the courtyard structure, and the fabrication of the Ark of the Covenant and the Table of Showbread. And they made the veil <note>original: "katapetasma" — the heavy inner curtain that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place</note> of blue <note>original: "hyakinthou" — a dye derived from murex snails, ranging from violet to deep blue</note> and purple and spun scarlet and fine twisted linen, a woven work of Cherubim <note>winged celestial beings who act as guardians of the divine presence</note>. # AND YOU SHALL ANOINT THE ALTAR

And the altar shall be **Holy of Holies**. And you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the doors of the **Tabernacle of Testimony** <note>original: "skenes tou martyriou" — also known as the Tent of Meeting, the portable sanctuary of the Israelites.</note> and you shall wash them with water. And you shall clothe Aaron in the holy garments and anoint him and sanctify him, and he shall serve as priest to me. And you shall bring his sons and clothe them in tunics and anoint them in the same manner as you anointed their <term>father</term> <note>original: "pra," an abbreviation for "patera" (father).</note>, and they shall serve as priests to me; and it shall be that their anointing shall be for an everlasting priesthood throughout their generations. 

And Moses did all things whatsoever the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "ks," an abbreviation for "Kyrios" (Lord).</note> commanded him; so he did. And it came to pass in the first month of the second year after their departure from Egypt, on the new moon, that the tabernacle was set up. And Moses set up the tabernacle, and placed its capitals, and inserted the bars, and set up its pillars. And he spread out the curtains over the tabernacle, and placed the covering of the tabernacle upon it from above, just as the <term>Lord</term> commanded Moses.

And taking the testimonies <note>original: "martyria" — the stone tablets of the Law.</note>, he put them into the ark, and placed the poles under the ark, and brought the ark into the tabernacle. And he placed the veil of the covering and shielded the ark of the testimony, in the same way the <term>Lord</term> commanded Moses. And he placed the table in the tabernacle of testimony, on the side of the tabernacle of testimony toward the north, outside the veil of the tabernacle, and set forth the **bread of presence** <note>original: "artous tes protheseos" — the twelve loaves of "showbread" displayed before God.</note> upon it before the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "ky," abbreviation for "Kyriou" (of the Lord).</note>, just as the <term>Lord</term> commanded Moses. And he placed the lampstand in the

<column-break/>

tabernacle of testimony on the side of the tabernacle toward the south, and he placed its lamps before the <term>Lord</term>, just as the <term>Lord</term> commanded Moses. And he placed the golden altar in the tabernacle of testimony in front of the veil, and he burned upon it the blended incense <note>original: "thymiana tes syntheseos" — a specific aromatic mixture of spices reserved for sacred use.</note>, in the same way the <term>Lord</term> commanded Moses.

And the altar of the whole-fruit offerings <note>original: "thysiasterion ton karpomaton" — the altar for burnt sacrifices.</note> he placed by the doors of the tabernacle of testimony.

And Moses finished all the works. And the cloud covered the tabernacle of testimony, and the tabernacle was filled with the **glory of the Lord**. And Moses was not able to enter into the tabernacle of testimony because the cloud overshadowed it, and the tabernacle was filled with the **glory of the Lord**. And whenever the cloud went up from the tabernacle, the sons of <term>Israel</term> <note>original: "iel," an abbreviation for "Israel."</note> would set out with their baggage. But if the cloud did not go up, they did not set out until the day the cloud went up. For a cloud was upon the tabernacle by day, and fire was upon it by night, in the sight of all **Israel** in all their departures.

And the **Lord** <note>original: "KS" (Kyrios) — the Lord.</note> spoke to **Moses**, saying: "Speak to the children of Israel, saying: You shall eat no **fat** <note>original: "stear" — specifically the hard internal fat or suet, which was reserved exclusively for the altar.</note> of oxen, or of sheep, or of goats. The fat of an animal that dies of itself, and the fat of that which is **torn by beasts**, may be used for any other purpose; but you shall by no means eat it. For whoever eats the fat of the animals from which one brings a **fruit-offering** <note>original: "karpōma" — a sacrifice offered by fire.</note> to the **Lord**, that soul shall be destroyed from among his people.

You shall eat **no blood** in any of your dwellings, whether it be of birds or of animals. Every soul that eats any blood, that soul shall be destroyed from among his people."

And the **Lord** spoke to **Moses**, saying: "Speak to the children of Israel, saying: He who offers his sacrifice of salvation to the **Lord** shall bring his gift to the **Lord** from the sacrifice of salvation. His own hands shall bring the fruit-offerings to the **Lord**; he shall bring the **fat** upon the breast-piece and the **lobe of the liver**, so as to present the gift before the **Lord**."

This is the law of the **burnt offerings**, and of the **grain offering**, and of the **sin offering**, and of the **guilt offering**, and of the **consecration** <note>original: "teleiōseōs" — literally "perfection" or "completion," referring to the ordination of priests.</note>, and of the sacrifice of salvation, just as the **Lord** commanded Moses on **Mount Sinai**, on the day he commanded the children of Israel to offer their gifts before the **Lord** in the **wilderness of Sinai**.

It emphasizes the strict seven-day period of consecration required before they could begin their full duties.</summary>

And these things are unclean to you among the swarming things that swarm upon the earth: the mouse and the land crocodile <note>original: "krokodilos ho chersaios" — likely referring to a large monitor lizard.</note>, the shrew-mouse <note>original: "mygalē"</note> and the chameleon, and the gecko <note>original: "kallabōtēs"</note> and the lizard and the skink <note>original: "chameuraala" — a rare term for a type of lizard</note>. In this way Aaron shall enter the Holy Place: with a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a whole-burnt offering. He shall put on the holy linen tunic and have linen undergarments upon his flesh, and he shall be girded with a linen sash and wear a linen **turban** <term>Turban</term> <note>original: *kidaris* — the distinctive head-covering of the High Priest.</note>. These are holy garments; and he shall wash his whole body in water [and then put them on]."

### The Laws for Priests

The **Lord** said to Moses, saying: "Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and you shall say to them: They shall not be defiled for a soul <note>original: "psychais"; here meaning a dead person or "corpse"</note> among their nation, except for the relative who is closest to him: for a father and mother, and for sons and daughters, and for a brother and a virgin sister who lives with him, who has not had a husband; for these he <unclear>may</unclear> be defiled. He shall not be defiled suddenly among his people to profane himself. And you shall not shave a bald spot on your head for the sake of any soul <note>referring again to mourning the dead</note>, nor shall they shave the appearance of their beard, nor shall they cut gashes into their flesh. They shall be holy to their **God** and shall not profane the name of their **God**, for they offer the sacrifices—the gifts of their **God**—and so they shall be holy.

They shall not take a woman who is a prostitute or profaned, nor shall they take a woman who has been cast out from her husband,

<column-break/>

for he is holy to the **Lord** his **God**. And you shall sanctify him, because he offers the gifts of the **Lord** your **God**. He shall be holy, for I, the **Lord** who sanctifies them, am holy.

And if the daughter of a man who is a priest is profaned by playing the prostitute, she profanes the name of her father <note>original: "PRC", a contraction of "Patros"</note>; she shall be burned with fire. 

### The Great Priest

The Great Priest <note>Referring to the High Priest</note> among his brothers, upon whose head the anointing oil <note>original: "elaiou tou christou"; literally "the oil of the Christ" or "the anointed oil"</note> has been poured and who has been consecrated to put on the holy garments, shall not remove his head-dress <note>original: "apokidarosei"; the "kidaris" was the formal priestly turban</note> from his head, nor shall he tear his clothes. He shall not go in to any dead soul <note>original: "psyche teteleutykyia"; a deceased person</note>; he shall not be defiled even for his father or for his mother. He shall not go out from the holy places, and he shall not profane the sanctuary of his **God**, because the holy anointing oil of **God** is upon him; I am the **Lord**.

He shall take a virgin of his own kin as a wife. A widow, or a cast-out woman, or a profaned woman, or a prostitute—these he shall not take. Instead, he shall take a virgin from his own people as a wife, and he shall not profane his seed among his nation; I am the **Lord** who sanctifies him."

### Regulations for Property and Servants

<column-break/>

[Houses in villages] which have no **wall** around them shall be reckoned as the fields of the land; they may be redeemed at any time, and they shall be released in the **Year of Release** <note>original: "ἄφεσις" (aphesis) — referring here to the Year of Jubilee where debts were forgiven and land returned to original owners</note>. 
**A**nd regarding the cities of the Levites, the houses in the cities of their possession shall be redeemable for the Levites at any time. And whatever a man redeems from the Levites, even the sale of a house in the city of their possession, it shall be released in the Year of Release; for the houses in the cities of the Levites are their inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel. But the fields set apart for their cities shall not be sold, for that is their eternal possession.
**I**f your brother becomes poor and his hands become weak among you, you shall help him as if he were a **proselyte** <note>original: "προσήλυτος" (proselytos) — a convert or stranger who has joined the community</note> or a **sojourner** <note>original: "πάροικος" (paroikos) — a resident alien or neighbor without full citizenship</note>, and your brother shall live with you. You shall not take interest from him, nor usury; but you shall fear your God, and your brother shall live with you. You shall not give him your money at interest, nor shall you give him your food for profit. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan, so as to be your God.
**I**f your brother among you becomes poor and is sold to you, you shall not make him serve with the service of a slave. He shall be with you as a hired servant or a sojourner; he shall work for you until the Year of Release. Then he shall depart from you, he and his children with him, and he shall go back to his own family and return to his paternal possession. For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as a slave is sold. You shall not oppress him with labor, but you shall fear the Lord your God.
**A**nd as for the male and female slaves who shall be yours from the nations that are around you, from them you may acquire a male or female slave, and from the children of the sojourners

<column-break/>

who dwell among you; from them you may acquire [slaves], and from their families who are born in your land; let these be your possession. And you may pass them as an inheritance to your children after you, and they shall be your property forever. But over your brothers, the children of Israel, no one shall oppress his brother with labor.
**I**f the hand of a proselyte or sojourner among you becomes rich, and your brother becomes poor and is sold to the proselyte or sojourner among you, or to a descendant of the family of the proselyte; after he is sold, there shall be a right of **redemption** <note>original: "λύτρωσις" (lytrosis) — the act of buying back a person or property</note> for him. One of his brothers may redeem him; his father's brother may redeem him, or the son of his father's brother may redeem him, or someone from his own close fleshly kin from his tribe may redeem him.
**I**f he becomes wealthy in his own hands, he may redeem himself. And he shall calculate with the one who bought him from the year he was sold to him until the Year of Release; and the price of his sale shall be according to the years, like the wages of a hired servant shall his time be with him. And if there are many years remaining, according to these he shall pay back the price of his redemption from the money for which he was sold. And if a few years are left until the Year of Release, he shall calculate for him according to his years, and he shall pay the price of his redemption. As a servant hired year by year he shall be with him; he shall not

# The Blessings of Obedience and the Curses of the Covenant

Neither shall a **carved stone** <note>original: "λίθον σκοπόν" (lithon skopon) — likely a figured stone or a stone set up for the purpose of worship or divination</note> be set up in your land to worship it. **M**y **Sabbaths** you shall keep, and my **holy things** you shall fear; I am the Lord your God.
**I**f you walk in my ordinances and keep my commandments and do them, I will give you rain in its season, and the land shall give its produce, and the trees of the plains shall yield their fruit. Your **harvest** shall overtake the **vintage**, and the vintage shall overtake the **sowing**; and you shall eat your bread to fullness, and you shall dwell with security upon your land.
**A**nd **war** shall not pass through your land. I will give **peace** in your land, and you shall sleep and there shall be no one to make you afraid. I will destroy evil beasts from your land, and war shall not pass through your land. You shall pursue your enemies, and they shall fall before you in slaughter. Five of you shall pursue a hundred, and a hundred of you shall pursue tens of thousands; and your enemies shall fall before you by the **sword**.
**A**nd I will look upon you and increase you, and I will multiply you, and I will establish my **covenant** with you. You shall eat the old and the very old, and you shall clear out the old to make room for the new. I will set my covenant among you, and my soul shall not abhor you. I will **walk among you**, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.
**I** am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt while you were **slaves**; I broke the bond of your **yoke** and led you forth with boldness.
**B**ut if you do not obey me, and do not perform these my ordinances, but disobey them, and your soul becomes weary of my judgments—

<column-break/>

—so that you do not perform all my commandments, but instead scatter my **covenant**, I also will do this to you: I will bring upon you **distress**, and the **itch** <note>original: "ψώρα" (psora) — a skin disease, mange, or scurvy</note>, and the **jaundice**, which waste away your eyes and cause your soul to pine away. You shall sow your seed in vain, and your enemies shall eat it. I will set my face against you, and you shall fall before your enemies.

### Chapter 27: Laws Concerning Vows
<margin>27</margin>**A**nd the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and you shall say to them: Whoever makes a **vow** as a value for his soul to the Lord, the valuation of a **male** from twenty years old until sixty years old shall be **fifty didrachmas of silver** <note>a standard silver coin; here equivalent to the biblical shekel</note> according to the holy weight.

...And for the female, the **valuation** <note>original: "συντίμησις" (syntimesis) — a formal estimate of worth or price</note> shall be **thirty didrachmas** <term>didrachma: a silver coin equivalent to two drachmas; in this context, it represents the Hebrew "shekel," the standard unit of weight and currency</term>.
**I**f the person is from five years old to twenty years old, the price for the male shall be twenty didrachmas, and for the female, ten didrachmas.
**F**rom one month old up to five years old, the price for the male shall be five didrachmas of silver, and for the female, three didrachmas.
**I**f from sixty years and upward: if it is a male, the valuation shall be fifteen didrachmas of silver; if a female, ten didrachmas.
**B**ut if the person is **too poor** for the valuation, he shall stand before the **priest**, and the priest shall value him; according to what the hands of the one who made the vow can afford, the priest shall value him.
**I**f the vow concerns **livestock** of the kind offered as a gift to the Lord, whatever one gives of these to the Lord shall be **holy**. He shall not exchange it, a good one for a bad one, nor a bad one for a good one. If he does indeed exchange animal for animal, both it and its substitute shall be holy.
**I**f, however, it is any **unclean animal** <margin>†</margin> that is not offered as a gift to the Lord, he shall set the animal before the priest. The priest shall value it between good and bad; as the priest values it, so shall it stand.
**B**ut if he wishes to **redeem** <note>original: "λυτρούμενος" (lytroumenos) — to buy back or ransom something dedicated to God</note> it, he shall add **one-fifth** <note>a 20% surcharge was standard for buying back dedicated property</note> to its valuation.
**A**nd if a man sanctifies his **house** as holy to the Lord, the priest shall value it between good and bad; as the priest values it, so it shall stand.
**I**f the one who sanctified it wishes to redeem his house, he shall add to it one-fifth of the silver, and it shall be his.
**I**f a man sanctifies to the Lord a part of the **field of his inheritance**, the valuation shall be according to its seed—a **homer** <note>original: "κόρου" (korou) — a dry measure of approximately 10 to 12 bushels</note> of barley seed...

...at **fifty didrachmas of silver**.
**I**f he sanctifies his field from the **Year of Release** <term>Year of Release: also known as the Jubilee (aphesis), a year occurring every 50 years when land returned to its original tribal owners</term>, it shall stand according to its valuation.
**B**ut if he sanctifies his field later, after the Release, the priest shall calculate the money for him according to the years that remain until the next Year of Release, and it shall be deducted from his valuation.
**I**f the one who sanctified the field wishes to redeem it, he shall add one-fifth of the silver of the price, and it shall be his.
**B**ut if he does not redeem the field and has sold the field to another man, it may no longer be redeemed. Rather, the field, when the Release comes, shall be **holy to the Lord**; like a field set apart, it shall be the possession of the priest.
**I**f he sanctifies to the Lord a field he has bought, which is not part of his inherited land, the priest shall calculate for him the total value until the Year of Release, and he shall pay the value on that day as a holy thing to the Lord.
**I**n the Year of Release, the field shall be returned to the man from whom he bought it, to whom the inheritance of the land belongs.
**A**ll valuations shall be according to the **holy weights** <note>original: "ὁλκαῖς ἁγίαις" (holkais hagiais) — standard weights kept in the sanctuary to ensure honest dealings</note>: twenty obols <note>original: "ὀβολοὶ" (oboloi) — a smaller unit of currency; 20 obols equal 1 shekel/didrachma</note> to the didrachma.
**E**very **firstborn** that is born among your livestock belongs to the Lord; no one shall sanctify it—whether calf or sheep, it is the Lord's.
**B**ut if it is among the unclean four-footed animals, he shall exchange it according to its valuation and add one-fifth to it, and he shall redeem it. If it is not redeemed, it shall be sold according to its valuation.
**E**very **devoted thing** <term>devoted thing: "anathema" in Greek; something set apart irrevocably for God, usually involving a ban on common use or a requirement for destruction</term> which a man devotes to the Lord from all that he has—from man to beast, and from the field of his inheritance—it shall not be sold nor redeemed. Every devoted thing shall be **most holy** to the Lord.
**A**nd every devoted thing that is devoted from among men...

<meta>This page continues the legal instructions found in the Book of Numbers. The previous page discussed the "water of the ordeal" used for a woman suspected of adultery. <margin>cross mark</margin>...be defiled if someone dies near him, because the vow <note>original: "ευχη" (euche) — a vow of consecration or a prayer-pledge.</note> of **God** <note>original: "Θυ" (Theou) — Nomina Sacra abbreviation for "of God."</note> is upon his head. All the days of his vow he shall be **holy to the Lord** <note>original: "κω" (Kyrio) — Nomina Sacra for "to the Lord."</note>. 

But if someone dies suddenly near him, the head of his vow shall be immediately defiled. He shall shave his head on the day he is cleansed; on the seventh day it shall be shaved. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the **priest**, to the doors of the **Tabernacle of the Testimony**. 

And the **priest** shall offer one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering; he shall make atonement for him regarding the things in which he sinned concerning his soul <note>In this context, "soul" refers to the person's life or state of ritual purity.</note>. He shall consecrate his head on that day in which he was sanctified to the **Lord** for the days of his vow, and he shall bring a yearling lamb for a guilt offering. The previous days shall be void, because the head of his vow was defiled.

<margin>—</margin> And this is the law for the one who has vowed: on the day he fulfills the days of his vow, he shall present himself at the doors of the **Tabernacle of the Testimony**. 

And he shall bring his gift to the **Lord**: one unblemished yearling male lamb for a burnt offering, and one unblemished yearling female lamb for a sin offering, and one unblemished ram for a peace offering <note>original: "σωτηριου" (soteriou) — literally "of salvation," often translated as "peace offering" in a sacrificial context.</note>. Also, a basket of unleavened bread of fine flour—loaves kneaded with oil and unleavened wafers smeared with oil—along with their grain offering and their drink offering. 

And the **priest** shall present them before the **Lord** and shall perform the ritual for his sin and his burnt offering. He shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace to the **Lord** with the basket of unleavened bread; the **priest** shall also perform his grain offering and his drink offering. 

Then the one who has vowed shall shave the head of his vow by the doors of the **Tabernacle of the Testimony**, and he shall put the hair upon the fire which is

<column-break/>

under the sacrifice of peace.

### Numbers 9:8—10:10

<column-break/>

But **Moses** said to them: "Stand here, and I will hear what the **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΣ" (Kyrios) — a common abbreviation for "Lord"</note> commands concerning you." And the **Lord** spoke to **Moses**, saying: "Speak to the sons of **Israel**, saying: 'If any man <note>original: "ΑΝΟΣ" (anthropos) — "human" or "person"</note> among you or your descendants becomes unclean because of a dead body, or is on a long journey, he shall still keep the **Passover** <note>original: "ΠΑΣΧΑ" (Pascha)</note> to the **Lord**.

They shall keep it in the second month, on the fourteenth day, toward evening; they shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. They shall leave none of it until morning, nor shall they break a bone of it; they shall perform it according to the law of the **Passover**. 

But any man who is clean and is not on a long journey, yet fails to keep the **Passover**, that soul shall be destroyed <note>meaning "cut off" or "excommunicated"</note> from among his people, because he did not bring the gift to the **Lord** at its appointed time; that man shall bear his sin. 

And if a proselyte <note>original: "ΠΡΟΣΗΛΥΤΟΣ" — a resident alien or convert</note> comes to you in your land and performs the **Passover** to the **Lord**, he shall do so according to the law of the **Passover** and according to its ordinance. There shall be one law for you, both for the stranger and for the native of the 

<margin>○</margin> land.'" And on the day that the **Tabernacle** was set up, the **cloud** covered the **Tabernacle**, the **House of Testimony**; and in the evening it was over the **Tabernacle** like the appearance of fire until morning. So it happened continually: the **cloud** covered it by day, and the appearance of fire by night. And whenever the **cloud** ascended from the **Tabernacle**, after that the sons of **Israel** would depart; and in the place where the **cloud** stood, there the sons of **Israel** would encamp. By the command of the **Lord** the sons of **Israel** would encamp, and by the command of the **Lord** they would depart; all the days that the **cloud** overshadowed the **Tabernacle**, the sons of **Israel** remained encamped. And when the **cloud** lingered over the **Tabernacle** for many days, then the sons of **Israel** kept the charge of the **God**

<column-break/>

and would not depart. And it was so when the **cloud** covered the **Tabernacle** for a specific number of days; according to the voice of the **Lord** they would encamp, and according to the command of the **Lord** they would depart. And it was so when the **cloud** remained from evening until morning, and the **cloud** ascended in the morning, they would depart; whether by day or by night, whenever the **cloud** ascended, they would depart. Whether it was for two days, or a month, or a longer time that the **cloud** overshadowed it, the sons of **Israel** remained encamped and would not depart; but when it ascended, they would depart. ### Numbers 22:12-35

And answering, **Balaam** said to the princes of **Balak**, "Even if **Balak** gave me his house full of silver or gold, I would not be able to transgress the word of the **Lord God** <note>original: "ΚΥ ΤΟΥ ΘΥ" (Kyriou tou Theou) — both words are abbreviated as sacred names.</note> to do it, whether small or great. Now, therefore, you also remain here this night, so that I may know what the **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΣ" (Kyrios)</note> will say to me further."

And **God** <note>original: "ΘΣ"</note> came to **Balaam** by night and said to him, "If these men have come to call you, rise and follow them; but only the word that I shall speak to you, this you shall do."

And **Balaam** rose in the morning, saddled his donkey, and went with the princes of **Moab**. And **God** was provoked with anger because he went, and the **Angel of God** <note>original: "ΑΓΓΕΛΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΘΥ"</note> stood in his way to **oppose** <note>original: "ενδιαβαλλειν" (endiaballein) — to stand against or accuse.</note> him on his journey.

Now he was riding upon his donkey, and his two servants were with him. And the donkey saw the **Angel of God** standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, and the donkey turned aside out of the road and went into the field. <column-break/>

And the **Angel of God** stood in a narrow path of the vineyards, with a wall on this side and a wall on that side. And when the donkey saw the **Angel of God**, she pressed herself against the wall and crushed **Balaam's** foot against the wall; and he struck her yet again.

And the **Angel of God** went further and stood in a narrow place where there was no way to turn to the right or to the left. And when the donkey saw the **Angel of God**, she lay down under **Balaam**. And **Balaam** was furious and struck the donkey with his staff.

And **God** opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to **Balaam**, "What have I done to you, that look, you have struck me this third time?"

And **Balaam** said to the donkey, "Because you have mocked me; and if I had a sword in my hand, I would have killed you by now!"

And the donkey said to **Balaam**, "Am I not your donkey, upon which you have ridden from your youth until this very day? Have I ever neglected you or acted toward you in this way before?" And he said, "No."

Then **God** opened the eyes of **Balaam**, and he saw the **Angel of the Lord** <note>original: "ΑΓΓΕΛΟΝ ΚΥ"</note> standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand; and he bowed down and prostrated himself on his face.

And the **Angel of God** said to him, "Why have you struck your donkey this third time? Behold, I came out to **oppose** you, because your way is not **pleasing** <note>original: "αστεια" (asteia) — often meaning 'proper' or 'fitting' in this context.</note> before me. And when the donkey saw me, she turned away from me these three times; and if she had not turned away from me, I would surely have killed you by now, but I would have spared her."

And **Balaam** said to the **Angel of the Lord**, "I have sinned, for I did not know that you were standing in the road against me. And now, if it is not pleasing to you, I will turn back."

But the **Angel of God** said to **Balaam**, "Go with the men; but only the word that I shall speak to you, this you shall be careful to speak."

And you shall bring **burnt offerings**, **offerings** for a **sweet-smelling savor**: **one bull**, **one ram**, **seven yearling lambs** without blemish; their **sacrifices** and their **drink offerings** for the **bull** and the **ram** and the **lambs** according to their **number**, according to their **ordinance**, and one **male kid from the goats** for **sin**, besides the **perpetual burnt offering**, their **sacrifices** and their **drink offerings**.
<margin>—</margin>
These things you shall do for the **Lord** <note>original: "KW" — sacred abbreviation for "Kuriō"</note> in your **feasts**, besides your **vows** <note>original: "euchōn"</note> and your **voluntary offerings** and your **burnt offerings** and your **sacrifices** and your **drink offerings** and your **peace offerings** <note>original: "sōtēria" — offerings for well-being or salvation</note>.
<margin>—</margin>
And **Moses** spoke to the **sons of Israel** <note>original: "IHL" — sacred abbreviation for "Israēl"</note> according to all that the **Lord** <note>original: "KC" — "Kurios"</note> commanded **Moses**. And **Moses** spoke to the **rulers of the tribes** of the **sons of Israel**, saying: "This is the **word** which the **Lord** commanded."
<margin>—</margin>
A **man** <note>original: "anthrōpos"</note> who **vows a vow** to the **Lord** or **swears an oath** or **binds himself** with a **binding obligation** <note>original: "orismō" — a boundary or limiting oath</note> concerning his **soul**, he shall not **profane his word**; everything that **comes out of his mouth**

<column-break/>

he shall do. But if a **woman** **vows a vow** to the **Lord** or **binds herself** with an **obligation** in the **house of her father** <note>original: "PRS" — "Patros"</note> in her **youth**, and her **father** <note>original: "PHR" — "Patēr"</note> **hears her vows** and her **obligations** which she **bound** upon her **soul**, and her **father** is **silent** toward her, then all her **vows shall stand**, and all her **obligations** which she **bound** upon her **soul** shall **remain** for her. But if her **father forbids her** on the day he **hears** her **vows** and her **obligations** which she **bound** upon her **soul**, they **shall not stand**; and the **Lord** shall **cleanse** <note>original: "katharisei" — or forgive/acquit</note> her because her **father forbade her**. And if she **belongs to a husband** <note>literally "if becoming, she becomes a man's"</note> and her **vows** are upon her according to the **utterance of her lips** <note>original: "diastolēn tōn cheileōn" — the distinct opening or expression of the lips</note> which she **bound** upon her **soul**, and her **husband hears** and is **silent** toward her on the day he **hears**, then all her **vows shall stand** and her **obligations** which she **bound** upon her **soul** shall **stand**. But if her **husband forbids her** on the day he **hears**, all her **vows** and her **obligations** which she **bound** upon her **soul** shall **not remain**, because her **husband forbade her**; and the **Lord** shall **cleanse** her.
<margin>—</margin>
The **vow of a widow** and one who is **cast out** <note>original: "ekbeblēmēnēs" — a divorced woman</note>, whatever she **vows** against her **soul** shall **remain** for her. But if her **vow** or her **obligation** against her **soul** was [made] **with an oath** in the **house of her husband**, and her **husband hears** and is **silent** toward her and **does not forbid her**, then all her **vows shall stand** and all the **obligations** which she **bound** against her **soul** shall **stand** for her. But if her **husband cancels them** <note>original: "ananeuōn ananeuse" — literally "refusing, he refuses" or "nodding no"</note> on the day he **hears**, everything that **comes out of her lips** concerning her **vows** and concerning her **obligations** against her **soul** shall **not remain**...

### Numbers 30:13 — 31:19

...her husband may confirm it, or her husband may void it <note>original: "perielei" — literally "to take away" or strip away the obligation</note>, regarding any oath taken to humble her soul. Every binding oath to afflict the soul, her husband shall establish it, or her husband shall void it.
But if he remains silent and says nothing to her day after day, then he confirms all her vows and all the obligations that are upon her; he has confirmed them because he remained silent to her on the day that he heard them.
But if he voids them some time after he has heard them, then he shall bear her guilt <note>original: "hamartian" — meaning the husband takes responsibility for the broken vow</note>.
These are the statutes which the **Lord** commanded **Moses** between a man and his wife, and between a father and his daughter in her youth, while she is still in her father’s house.

<margin>31</margin>
And the **Lord** spoke to **Moses**, saying: "Avenge the children of **Israel** against the **Midianites** <note>The Midianites had previously led the Israelites into idolatry and immorality at Peor</note>, and afterward you shall be gathered to your people" <note>A biblical idiom for death</note>.
And **Moses** spoke to the people, saying: "Arm some of your men for war and let them go against **Midian** to carry out the **Lord’s** vengeance on **Midian**. You shall send a thousand from every tribe, from all the tribes of **Israel**, to the war."
So there were recruited from the thousands of **Israel**, a thousand from every tribe—twelve thousand armed for war.
And **Moses** sent them, a thousand from every tribe, along with **Phinehas** <note>The grandson of Aaron, known for his religious zeal</note> the son of **Eleazar** the priest, to the assembly, carrying the holy vessels and the signaling trumpets in his hands.
And they went to war against **Midian**, just as the **Lord** had commanded **Moses**, and they killed every male.
They also killed the kings of **Midian** along with the rest of their slain: **Evi**, **Rekem**, **Zur**, **Hur**, and **Reba**, the five kings of **Midian**. They also killed **Balaam** <note>The prophet who had previously tried to curse Israel</note> the son of **Beor** with the sword among their slain.
The children of **Israel** took the women of **Midian** as captives, along with their goods and their cattle,

<column-break/>

and all their livestock; and they took all their wealth as spoil. They burned all the cities where they dwelt and all their encampments with fire.
They took all the spoil and all the prey, both of people and of livestock. Then they brought the captives, the prey, and the spoil to **Moses**, to **Eleazar** the priest, and to all the children of **Israel**, at the camp in the **plains of Moab** <note>original: "Arbath-Moab"</note> which is by the **Jordan** across from **Jericho**.
Then **Moses**, **Eleazar** the priest, and all the leaders of the congregation went out to meet them outside the camp.
But **Moses** was angry with the officers of the army—the captains of thousands and captains of hundreds—who had come back from the battle.
**Moses** said to them: "Why have you kept every female alive? For these were the ones who, following the advice of **Balaam**, caused the children of **Israel** to rebel and turn away from the word of the **Lord** in the matter of **Peor** <note>referring to the incident at Baal-Peor where Israel fell into idolatry</note>, and the plague came upon the congregation of the **Lord**.
Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known a man intimately. But all the young girls who have not known a man intimately, keep alive for yourselves.
And as for you, encamp outside the camp for seven days; whoever has killed any person and whoever has touched anyone slain, you must purify yourselves on the third day and on the seventh day."

# Deuteronomy 14:17—15:10

And it shall be, if you are not pleased with her, you shall let her go free; you shall not sell her for money. You shall not treat her as a slave because you have humbled her.

### If a Man Has Two Wives
If a man has two wives, one loved and one hated, and they both bear him children—both the loved and the hated—and the firstborn son belongs to the hated wife; then on the day he bequeaths his possessions to his sons, he cannot grant the birthright to the son of the loved wife, overlooking the son of the hated wife, who is the actual firstborn. Instead, he must recognize the firstborn, the son of the hated wife, by giving him a double portion of all that he has; for he is the beginning of his children, and to him belongs the right of the firstborn <term>birthright</term><note>the "prototokeia," referring to the legal and spiritual status of the eldest son</note>.

### If Someone Has a Stubborn and Rebellious Son
If someone has a stubborn and rebellious son who does not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and though they discipline him, he does not listen to them; then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city and to the gate of his place. And they shall say to the men of his city, "This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard." Then all the men of his city shall stone him to death with stones. Thus you shall remove the evil from among yourselves, and all the rest, when they hear of it, shall be afraid.

### If There Is a Sin Worthy of Death
If there is in someone a sin worthy of the judgment of death, and he is put to death,

<column-break/>

and you hang him on a tree: his body shall not remain overnight upon the tree, but you shall surely bury him on that same day; for everyone who is hanged on a tree is cursed by **God** <note>original: "THU," Nomen Sacrum for "Theou"</note>. And you shall not defile the land which the **Lord your God** <note>original: "KS O THS," Nomina Sacra for "Kyrios ho Theos"</note> gives to you as an inheritance.

<margin>22.</margin> ### Concerning Lost Property
You shall not see your brother's calf or his sheep wandering on the road and ignore them; 
<margin>Restoration</margin> you shall surely return them to your brother. 
<margin>Return</margin> If your brother is not near you, or if you do not know him, you shall bring them into your house, and they shall stay with you until your brother seeks them, and you shall give them back to him. You shall do the same with his donkey, and you shall do the same with his garment, and you shall do the same with every lost thing of your brother's which is lost by him and found by you; you cannot ignore it.

### Helping a Fallen Animal
You shall not see your brother's donkey or his calf fallen on the road; you must not ignore them. You shall help him lift them up. 
A woman shall not wear a man's items, nor shall a man put on a woman's robe; for everyone who does these things is an abomination to **your God**.

<margin>You shall</margin> ### Kindness to Mother Birds
<margin>surely</margin> If you happen to come upon a bird's nest before you on the 
<margin>send away</margin> road, in any tree or on the ground, with young ones or eggs, and the mother is sitting on the young or on the eggs, you shall not take the mother with the young. You shall surely let the mother go, but the young you may take for yourself, so that it may go well with you and you may live a long time.

### Safety in Building
If you build a new house, you shall make a parapet <note>a low protective wall or railing</note> for your roof, so that you do not bring blood-guilt upon your house if someone should fall from it.

### Diverse Sowing and Plowing
You shall not plant your vineyard with different kinds of seed, lest the fruit be defiled—both the seed which you have sown and the fruit of your vineyard. You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.

### Laws Regarding Marriage and Purity
If a man takes a wife and lives with her, but then grows to hate her and brings false charges against her, giving her a bad name by saying, "I took this woman, but when I approached her, I did not find the evidence of her virginity"; then the father and the mother of the young woman shall take the evidence of the young woman's virginity <note>the "tokens of virginity" usually refers to a blood-stained cloth from the wedding night</note> and bring it to the elders of the city at the gate. 

And the father of the young woman shall say to the elders, "I gave my daughter to this man as a wife, and now he hates her and brings false charges, saying, 'I did not find evidence of your daughter's virginity.' But here is the evidence of my daughter's virginity." And they shall spread the garment before the elders of the city. 

Then the elders of that city shall take that man and discipline him; they shall fine him one hundred shekels <term>shekel</term><note>a standard unit of weight for silver used in trade and fines</note> and give them to the father of the young woman, because that man brought an evil name upon a virgin of Israel. She shall remain his wife; he may not divorce her all his days.

But if the charge is true, and the evidence of virginity was not found for the young woman, then they shall bring the young woman out to the doors of her father’s house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones until she dies, because she has committed an act of disgrace in Israel by playing the harlot in her father’s house. Thus you shall purge the evil from among yourselves.

If a man is found sleeping with a woman who is married to a husband, you shall kill both of them—the man

<column-break/>

who slept with the woman and the woman herself. Thus you shall purge the evil from Israel.

### Laws Regarding Seduction and Rape
If there is a young woman who is a virgin betrothed to a man, and a man finds her in the city and sleeps with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of their city and stone them with stones until they die; the young woman because she did not cry out for help while in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor’s wife. Thus you shall purge the evil from among yourselves.

But if the man finds the betrothed young woman in the open field and the man forces her and sleeps with her, then you shall kill only the man who slept with her. You shall do nothing to the young woman; there is no sin in the young woman deserving of death. For this case is like when a man rises up against his neighbor and murders him; so is this matter. For he found her in the field; the betrothed young woman cried out, but there was no one to help her.

If a man finds a young woman who is a virgin and is not betrothed, and he seizes her and sleeps with her, and they are discovered, the man who slept with her shall give fifty drachmas <note>original: "drachma," a Greek silver coin used here to translate the Hebrew silver weight</note> of silver to the father of the young woman, and she shall be his wife because he violated her; he may not divorce her all his days.

A man shall not take his father’s wife, and he shall not uncover his father’s covering <note>original: "syngalymma," a euphemism for the father's bed or sexual privacy</note>.

## CALEB’S INHERITANCE AND THE BORDERS OF JUDAH

...concerning me and you in Kadesh-Barnea. For I was forty years old when Moses, the servant of the Lord <note>original: "KY," a contraction for *Kyriou* (of the Lord), used as a sacred name.</note>, sent me to spy out the land, and I brought back word to him according to his own mind. But my brothers who went up with me turned away the heart of the people; yet I set myself to follow the Lord my God <note>original: "KŌ TŌ THŌ," contractions for *Kyriō tō Theō* (the Lord the God).</note>. And Moses swore on that day, saying: "The land on which you set foot shall be yours as an inheritance and for your children forever, because you set yourself to follow after the Lord our God."

And now, behold, the Lord has kept me alive just as he said. This is the forty-fifth year since the Lord spoke this word to Moses, while Israel journeyed in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am today eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as when Moses sent me; as my strength was then, so it is now to go out and to enter into war. And now, give me this mountain, just as the Lord spoke on that day. For you heard this word on that day; now behold, the Anakim <note>The Anakim were a race of legendary giants whose presence terrified the original spies.</note> are there, with cities that are fortified and great. If then the Lord is with me, I shall utterly destroy them, just as the Lord said to me.

And Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as an inheritance. Already <unclear> . . . </unclear> Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as an inheritance. <insert>For this reason,</insert> Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite until this very day, because he followed the command of the Lord the God of Israel. Now the name of Hebron was previously the City of Argob <note>original: "Polis Argob," usually identified as Kiriath-arba in other translations.</note>, the metropolis of the Anakim.

And the land had rest from war.

And it proceeds across from the Ascent of Akrabbim <note>literally "Scorpion Pass."</note> and passes around Zin, and goes up from the south to Kadesh-Barnea. These are their borders from the south.

A standard legal practice or decree.</note> in former times in Israel regarding the right of redemption and regarding an exchange to confirm every matter: a man would take off his sandal and give it to his neighbor; and this was a testimony in Israel.
And the kinsman-redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," and he took off his sandal and gave it to him.
<margin>K</margin>And Boaz said to the elders and to all the people, "You are witnesses today that I have bought all that belonged to Abimelech and all that belonged to Chaileon <note>original: "Chaileōn." Commonly known as Chilion.</note> and Mahlon <note>original: "Maalōn."</note> from the hand of Naomi. 
<margin>K</margin>And also Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, I have acquired for myself as a wife, to raise up the name of the deceased upon his inheritance, so that the name of the deceased will not be destroyed from among his brothers and from the tribe of his people. You are witnesses today."

<summary>This page describes the legal negotiation at the city gate where Boaz convinces a closer relative to yield his redemption rights, allowing Boaz to marry Ruth and restore the family's land. The text records the ancient Israelite custom of removing a sandal to seal a contract and the public blessing of the marriage by the elders.</summary>

And all the people in the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses! May the Lord grant that your wife, who is entering into your house, be as Rachel and as Leah, who both built the house of Israel; and may she act with power in Ephrathah <note>Ephrathah is an ancient name for the region surrounding Bethlehem, often used in poetic or formal contexts.</note> and may her name be famous in Bethlehem. And may your house be like the house of Pharez <note>original: "Phares." Pharez was the son of Judah and Tamar, and the ancestor of the tribe of Judah settled in Bethlehem.</note>, whom Tamar bore to Judah, from the offspring which the Lord shall give you from this young woman."

And Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the Lord gave her conception, and she bore a son. And the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the Lord, who has not left you today without a redeemer <note>original: "gonēa." This refers to the kinsman-redeemer who ensures the family line continues.</note>. May your name be called in Israel! And he shall be to you a restorer of your soul and a nourisher of your old age; for your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has born him."

And Naomi took the child and laid him in her bosom and became a nurse to him. And the neighbor women gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi!" And they called his name Obed; he is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
